text: Henri de Valois, duc d'Angoulême (1551 – 2 June 1586, in Aix-en-Provence), also known as "Henri, bâtard de Valois" or "Henri de France," was a Légitimé de France, cleric, and military commander during the Wars of Religion. He was born the bastard son of Henri II of France and his mistress Janet Stewart, Lady Fleming, an illegitimate daughter of James IV of Scotland. As the most favored natural son of the king, he was legitimized and granted the title of Duke of Angoulême. Henri served as Abbot of La Chaise-Dieu, Grand Prior of France of the Sovereign Order of Malta, and Admiral of the Levantine Sea, and ruled as Governor of Provence from 1579 until his death in 1586. In 1570, supporters of Mary, Queen of Scots, selected Henri as a potential leader of a French military force to assist them in their civil war against James VI of Scotland, believing his Scottish and French royal ancestry would earn him respect in Scotland and England; however, the plan was proposed to John Lesley, Queen Mary's ambassador in France, and ultimately, French soldiers and Henri were not sent to Scotland. Henri played a major role in the two prolonged military campaigns against Huguenot strongholds during the peak of the French Wars of Religion, participating in the Siege of La Rochelle (1572–1573), organized by the Duke of Anjou, future King Henry III of France, and leading the five-year Siege of Ménerbes (1573–1578), which took place at a citadel in the Luberon foothills favored by Pope Pius V. While serving as Governor of Provence, his secretary was the poet François de Malherbe, and Henri composed many sonnets, one of which was set to music by Fabrice Caietain. In 1586, Henri was killed in a duel at Aix-en-Provence with Philip Altoviti, who was also mortally wounded in the encounter.
